title: Google Cloud Certified Generative AI Leader

nodes.title: Google Vertex AI (PDE / PCA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Vertex AI is GCP's unified ML platform — it replaces AI Platform, AutoML, and several standalone services under one API surface. PDE and PCA exams test Feature Store for feature reuse, Model Registry for versioning, Pipelines for reproducibility, and the trade-offs between AutoML and custom training.

flashcards.front: AutoML vs custom training on Vertex AI — when do you choose each?
flashcards.back: AutoML: no ML code required — provide labeled data, Vertex trains and optimizes a model for you. Best for teams without ML expertise or for tabular/vision/NLP tasks where a proven architecture suffices. Custom training: bring your own code (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn) in a custom container — required when you need a specific architecture, preprocessing logic, or domain-specific objectives that AutoML doesn't expose.

flashcards.front: Vertex AI Feature Store — what problem does it solve?
flashcards.back: Feature Store is a centralized, managed repository for ML features. It solves training–serving skew (the exact same feature computation is used for both offline training and online inference), enables feature reuse across teams and models, and provides point-in-time correct lookups to avoid data leakage. Features are stored as entity–feature–timestamp tuples and can be served online (low-latency) or offline (batch).

flashcards.front: Vertex AI Model Registry vs Endpoint — what is each?
flashcards.back: Model Registry: versioned catalog of trained model artifacts — stores metadata, lineage, and performance metrics. Uploading a model here doesn't serve it. Endpoint: a deployed, load-balanced serving resource that routes prediction requests to one or more model versions. You import a model from the Registry into an Endpoint to serve traffic; a single endpoint can hold multiple model versions with traffic splits for A/B testing.

flashcards.front: Online prediction vs batch prediction — pick the right one.
flashcards.back: Online prediction: real-time, low-latency (< 200 ms) REST calls against a deployed Endpoint — use when a user or application needs an immediate answer. Batch prediction: Vertex reads a BigQuery table or GCS file, runs inference on all rows, writes results back — use for scheduled scoring of large datasets where latency is not a constraint. Batch is significantly cheaper per prediction.

questions.q: A team wants a single Google Cloud managed platform to prompt Gemini, browse open and partner foundation models, tune them, and deploy production prediction endpoints. Which service best fits?
choices: Vertex AI, which unifies Vertex AI Studio, Model Garden, tuning, and prediction endpoints under one managed platform.
Cloud Functions, an event-driven compute runtime for short serverless functions.
Cloud SQL, a managed relational database service for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server.
Cloud Interconnect, which provides private network connectivity between on-premises and Google Cloud.
questions.explanation: Vertex AI is the umbrella managed AI/ML platform on Google Cloud. Vertex AI Studio provides prompt design and testing for Gemini, Model Garden is the curated catalog of Google, partner, and open-source foundation models, and Vertex AI Prediction serves tuned or off-the-shelf models behind managed endpoints — all in one place. Cloud Functions is a general-purpose event-driven compute service; it does not host or catalog foundation models. Cloud SQL is a managed relational database and has no generative AI surface. Cloud Interconnect provides private network links between on-premises data centers and Google Cloud and is unrelated to model development.

questions.q: A high-volume customer support workflow needs the most cost- and latency-efficient Gemini tier that still handles multimodal inputs. Which model tier is the recommended starting point?
choices: Gemini Ultra, the highest-capability tier positioned for the most complex reasoning tasks.
Gemini Nano, which is designed to run entirely on-device rather than in a data center.
Gemini Flash, the multimodal tier engineered for high-volume, cost- and latency-sensitive workloads.
PaLM 2 text-bison, Google's earlier text-only foundation model that predates the Gemini family.
questions.explanation: Gemini Flash is explicitly positioned by Google as the fast, cost-efficient multimodal tier for high-volume production traffic where latency and price per token matter more than pushing every reasoning benchmark. Gemini Ultra targets the most complex reasoning and is the most expensive tier — the opposite of the constraint here. Gemini Nano is optimized for on-device use (for example inside Android or Chrome) rather than a server-side support workflow. PaLM 2 text-bison is Google's earlier, text-only foundation model that has been superseded by the Gemini family and lacks native multimodal input.

questions.q: What is the primary role of Vertex AI Model Garden?
choices: It automatically retrains deployed models every night against fresh training data.
It provides a Kubernetes autoscaler dedicated to GPU inference workloads.
It stores labeled datasets and versions them for supervised training.
It offers a curated catalog of Google, third-party, and open-source foundation models that customers can discover, evaluate, tune, and deploy from one place.
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Model Garden is Google Cloud's catalog of foundation models — first-party Google models (Gemini, Imagen, Chirp, Codey), partner models (for example Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, Mistral), and popular open-source models — with a consistent experience for exploration, evaluation, tuning, and one-click deployment. It does not by itself run a scheduled retraining pipeline; retraining is a Vertex AI Pipelines / Training concern. It is not a GKE autoscaler; scaling is handled by Vertex AI Prediction endpoints. And it is not a dataset store — labeled data belongs in Vertex AI Datasets or Cloud Storage / BigQuery.

questions.q: A retailer wants to deploy a customer-facing conversational assistant grounded in its help-center content with minimal custom code. Which Google Cloud product is the best fit?
choices: Cloud Dataproc, a managed Apache Spark and Hadoop service used for batch data processing.
Vertex AI Agent Builder (Conversational Agents), grounded on the help center through Vertex AI Search.
Compute Engine, using a single VM to host an open-source model server.
Cloud Storage lifecycle policies that move objects between storage classes on a schedule.
questions.explanation: Vertex AI Agent Builder — including the Conversational Agents experience — is Google Cloud's low-code way to build enterprise conversational and agentic experiences, and it integrates natively with Vertex AI Search so answers stay grounded in a specific corpus (a help center, a product catalog). Cloud Dataproc runs Spark and Hadoop batch jobs; it is not a conversational front end. Standing up a VM on Compute Engine with an open-source model server pushes all the assistant logic, scaling, and grounding onto the team — the opposite of "minimal custom code." Cloud Storage lifecycle policies are about object retention and cost tiering; they have nothing to do with building an assistant.

questions.q: Which Google product embeds generative AI directly inside productivity apps such as Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Meet?
choices: Cloud Deploy, a managed continuous-delivery service for GKE, Cloud Run, and other runtimes.
Gemini for Google Workspace, which brings Gemini-powered assistance into Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Meet.
Cloud Interconnect, which provides private network connectivity between on-premises and Google Cloud.
Anthos Config Management, which enforces declarative policy and configuration across Kubernetes fleets.
questions.explanation: Gemini for Google Workspace is the productization of Gemini inside Workspace apps — Help me write in Gmail and Docs, generation and analysis in Sheets, image and layout help in Slides, note taking and translation in Meet. Cloud Deploy is a CI/CD delivery service for Kubernetes and serverless runtimes; it does not sit inside Gmail or Docs. Cloud Interconnect is a networking product for private connectivity to Google Cloud and has no productivity-app surface. Anthos Config Management enforces declarative configuration across Kubernetes clusters and is unrelated to end-user productivity applications.

nodes.title: Techniques: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Techniques. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A retail chatbot must answer questions using the company's private product catalog and cite the source document for each answer. Which approach fits best?
flashcards.back: Retrieval Augmented Generation retrieves the most relevant private-catalog passages at query time, passes them to the model as grounded context, and lets the answer cite the retrieved document — exactly what the requirement asks. Vertex AI Search provides the enterprise-grade retrieval layer for this pattern. Raising temperature affects randomness, not factual grounding, and typically hurts accuracy. Zero-shot prompting of a public model gives the chatbot no access to the private catalog, so answers will be generic or hallucinated. Fine-tuning on generic transcripts teaches style but does not inject the specific product data or produce citations, and it must be redone every time the catalog changes.

flashcards.front: A team's summarization prompts return inconsistent formats and lengths. Without training a new model, what is the most effective first improvement?
flashcards.back: Prompt engineering — a precise instruction plus a handful of representative input/output examples — is the highest-leverage lever before spending on training. Few-shot examples anchor the desired format and length far more reliably than natural-language description alone. Reducing the context window does not change formatting behavior and can drop the very examples you would need. Raising temperature makes outputs less consistent, not more. Randomly rerolling until something looks right is not a repeatable engineering practice, does not scale, and wastes tokens and latency.

flashcards.front: When is supervised fine-tuning of a foundation model the most appropriate technique?
flashcards.back: Supervised fine-tuning shifts a model's weights toward a specific behavior, style, or format using a curated set of labeled input/output pairs. It is worth the cost when prompting and RAG cannot meet quality bars and you have the labeled data. Constantly changing data is a poor fit for fine-tuning — retraining nightly is expensive; RAG on a live index is the standard answer instead. Fine-tuning is by definition supervised, so it requires labeled examples; wanting a task solved with none of them points to prompting or unsupervised techniques, not fine-tuning. And fine-tuning does not give a model live internet access — grounding tools such as Vertex AI Search or Grounding with Google Search fill that role.

flashcards.front: To power semantic search over an enterprise document corpus, what is the fundamental technique required?
flashcards.back: Semantic search relies on embeddings: a text-embeddings model turns each chunk into a dense vector so that semantically similar text lives close together in vector space, and a vector database such as Vertex AI Vector Search returns nearest neighbors for a query embedding. LIKE queries in Cloud SQL only match literal substrings and miss paraphrased or conceptually related content — the opposite of semantic. MD5 is a cryptographic hash whose outputs are uncorrelated with meaning, so it can identify duplicates but says nothing about similarity. Compressing with gzip changes the byte layout without exposing any semantic signal and cannot power similarity search.

questions.q: A retail chatbot must answer questions using the company's private product catalog and cite the source document for each answer. Which approach fits best?
choices: Increase the model's temperature so answers feel more creative and diverse.
Rely on zero-shot prompting of a public Gemini model with no additional context.
Fine-tune the base model on generic customer-service transcripts collected from the public web.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) that grounds the model on the private catalog through Vertex AI Search and returns the retrieved snippets as citations.
questions.explanation: Retrieval Augmented Generation retrieves the most relevant private-catalog passages at query time, passes them to the model as grounded context, and lets the answer cite the retrieved document — exactly what the requirement asks. Vertex AI Search provides the enterprise-grade retrieval layer for this pattern. Raising temperature affects randomness, not factual grounding, and typically hurts accuracy. Zero-shot prompting of a public model gives the chatbot no access to the private catalog, so answers will be generic or hallucinated. Fine-tuning on generic transcripts teaches style but does not inject the specific product data or produce citations, and it must be redone every time the catalog changes.

questions.q: A team's summarization prompts return inconsistent formats and lengths. Without training a new model, what is the most effective first improvement?
choices: Reduce the model's context window so it is physically unable to produce long output.
Increase the temperature to 1.0 to encourage more variety in the output.
Rewrite the prompt to include a clear instruction and 2-3 few-shot examples that demonstrate the desired output format.
Regenerate the response repeatedly and randomly discard any output whose format looks wrong.
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering — a precise instruction plus a handful of representative input/output examples — is the highest-leverage lever before spending on training. Few-shot examples anchor the desired format and length far more reliably than natural-language description alone. Reducing the context window does not change formatting behavior and can drop the very examples you would need. Raising temperature makes outputs less consistent, not more. Randomly rerolling until something looks right is not a repeatable engineering practice, does not scale, and wastes tokens and latency.

questions.q: When is supervised fine-tuning of a foundation model the most appropriate technique?
choices: When the model must consistently adopt a specialized tone, format, or task behavior that prompt engineering and RAG cannot reliably achieve, and you have curated labeled examples.
When your ground-truth data changes hour by hour and the model must always reflect the latest state.
When you cannot label any examples at all and want the model to figure the task out on its own.
When you need the model to look up new facts on the public internet at inference time.
questions.explanation: Supervised fine-tuning shifts a model's weights toward a specific behavior, style, or format using a curated set of labeled input/output pairs. It is worth the cost when prompting and RAG cannot meet quality bars and you have the labeled data. Fine-tuning is by definition supervised, so it requires labeled examples; wanting a task solved with none of them points to prompting or unsupervised techniques, not fine-tuning. And fine-tuning does not give a model live internet access — grounding tools such as Vertex AI Search or Grounding with Google Search fill that role.

questions.q: To power semantic search over an enterprise document corpus, what is the fundamental technique required?
choices: Encode documents with a text-embeddings model (for example text-embedding-004) and query the resulting vectors with Vertex AI Vector Search.
Store the raw PDFs in Cloud SQL and run SQL LIKE queries against the extracted text column.
Compute an MD5 hash of every document and index the hashes for lookup.
Compress each document with gzip before storing it and search the compressed bytes.
questions.explanation: Semantic search relies on embeddings: a text-embeddings model turns each chunk into a dense vector so that semantically similar text lives close together in vector space, and a vector database such as Vertex AI Vector Search returns nearest neighbors for a query embedding. LIKE queries in Cloud SQL only match literal substrings and miss paraphrased or conceptually related content — the opposite of semantic. MD5 is a cryptographic hash whose outputs are uncorrelated with meaning, so it can identify duplicates but says nothing about similarity. Compressing with gzip changes the byte layout without exposing any semantic signal and cannot power similarity search.
